1	# Task 10: Desert canyon at dusk with slow camera flythrough
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite. It must render one full-viewport canvas with id #app. The scene is a desert canyon at dusk: tall layered sandstone walls on both sides of a winding dry riverbed, warm orange and magenta low sun near the horizon, a cool blue-violet sky gradient overhead, long soft shadows, and a few scattered boulders and dead shrubs on the canyon floor. Fine atmospheric haze should make distant walls fade toward the sky colour. The camera performs a slow, smooth, looping flythrough along the canyon floor at roughly eye height, gently drifting left and right, with no user input needed. Do not rely on any external image or model downloads; build everything procedurally or from assets the framework already provides. The page must show no console errors and must keep rendering continuously.

content.thinking: I'm wondering whether app.camera is reliably defined for perspective scenes, since calling setPose each frame risks hitting undefined if the AuraCameraController isn't initialized yet. I should check the CameraController implementation to see exactly when it becomes available before deciding on a fallback approach.

I should call app.camera.setPose with position and target each frame using a cut, so let me quickly check the setPose implementation to see if it has overrides or smoothing behavior I need to account for.

I'll keep setPose active each frame instead of cutting, so temporal history stays intact for the controller. Now I'm thinking through the canyon geometry as a custom heightfield mesh with per-vertex coloring.

For looping, I need the canyon's meander pattern to be periodic along z with period P, so the camera can wrap seamlessly. I'll set P to 120, extend the mesh well beyond that range so the far end fades into fog before the wrap point, and generate boulders and shrubs periodically across the same span so nothing pops in or out at the seam.

I'm settling on a strip width of roughly 140m across and 300m long at 1.5m cell resolution, giving around 19k vertices which stays comfortably under index limits. Walls will be steep (25-35m tall) with vertex colors banded by height and warped by noise for a layered sandstone look, though at this resolution the bands will need smooth blending to avoid looking blocky.

Rather than relying on height-based color banding alone, which aliases badly on steep walls since adjacent vertices can differ by several meters, I'm thinking of actually terracing the wall geometry itself -- giving it a stepped, ledge-like profile similar to real canyon strata, so the layered look comes from the shape rather than just the coloring.

I'm also weighing whether a custom per-pixel shader for the banding would look cleaner than vertex-based terracing, though that carries more implementation risk.

Vertex colors with terraces plus noise-based variation feels like the safer path. For the canyon shape itself, I'm sketching a winding centerline using layered sine waves with a period around 200, with a half-width that also oscillates to give the walls some organic variation.

For the floor, I'm carving a shallow sinuous riverbed channel into the center, colored pale sand with a darker pebbly stripe, while the wall heights rise from the channel distance with a steep slope that eventually plateaus near the canyon's outer edges.

I'm adding noise to make the walls jagged like buttresses, then quantizing the raw height into terraced steps — roughly 5.5m layers with flat ledges and smooth cliff faces between them, capping near the plateau height. I'm noting that at 1.2m cell resolution these terrace steps may still show aliasing artifacts.

With a gentler wall slope, each terrace step spans about 5m horizontally — a 2.2m ledge and a 2.8m cliff climbing 5.5m, giving a 63° slope that should render cleanly at 1m resolution. I'm sizing the canyon so 34m walls sit about 40m from center, with the centerline wandering ±17m, meaning from inside the canyon at eye level the walls dominate the view and the sky only peeks through as a narrow strip overhead.

Rather than that extreme, I'll scale it back: 26m walls with a 28m-wide floor gives a 60° elevation angle at 15m distance, which pairs better with a slightly pitched camera and ~50° vertical FOV so the sky stays mostly visible ahead. I'm putting the sun low near the horizon roughly along the canyon axis, around 6° elevation and slightly off to the left, so it's mostly blocked by the walls as the camera flies toward it through the winding canyon — leaving the floor in shadow while the upper ledges catch warm orange light for a dusky, atmospheric look, and I'm adding a hemisphere light for a cool blue-violet fill.

For lighting setup, I'm choosing to author the sky, hemisphere light, directional sun with shadows, and fog manually rather than relying on a preset like "golden-hour," since I want finer control over the look; I need to remember that authored lights without an environment won't get image-based lighting, so I should add a sky gradient with capture environment enabled to supply that. I'm leaning toward a gradient sky with a deep blue-violet zenith, an orange-magenta horizon, and a thin magenta band near the sun's elevation for that golden-hour glow, though I'm still working out the right intensity scale for the color bands.

For fog, I want the haze color to roughly match the horizon's orange-magenta tone so distant walls blend naturally into the sky rather than clashing, so I'm settling on a dusty pink-violet tone. Since I can't actually render anything to test density values, I need to be conservative with the fog density—something like 0.008—and pick a reasonable camera far plane (400) since I can only typecheck, not visually tune the scene.

Now I'm working out mesh geometry: the camera travels in -z, wraps around a track of length P, and with fog density 0.008 visibility extends roughly 250-300m before the wrap becomes noticeable. I'm sizing the floor mesh to span from -300 to P+30 in z to cover the visible range plus wraparound, using a 2.0m z-cell and 1.25m x-cell to keep vertex/triangle counts reasonable (~70k triangles) for a software-rendered WebGL context.

Rethinking this, I'll shrink the setup: with P=160 and a 260m view distance, z spans -260 to 190, giving about 225 rows at 2m spacing. I'm checking the fog math again — at 260m the exp2 falloff leaves visibility near 0.4%, but a basic exponential fog leaves about 10%, which could reveal a thin edge of terrain against the sky at the mesh boundary. Since fog blends toward the horizon color, this edge should be nearly invisible as long as the fog color matches the horizon, and beyond that the canyon walls are tall enough to mask the terrain's far cutoff anyway.

Now I'm working out the camera path: it loops with period P=160, with the centerline following a sine drift and the look-target sampled 12m ahead along the same drifting path so turns stay smooth. I'm picking a slow speed around 3 m/s, which gives a loop time of about 53 seconds, and setting eye height around 1.8m with a gentle vertical bob. Since all the lateral drift terms are harmonics of the terrain period P, the camera motion wraps seamlessly with no visible seam at the loop point.

For coloring, I'm cycling through a sandstone palette of reds, oranges, and tans per rock layer with some hashed noise, darkening near wall bases and crevices for a soft ambient-occlusion effect, and I'm deciding to keep lighting warm and low like sunset without overthinking the sRGB vs linear color space question. Surface normals come from finite-differencing the height function analytically, and that height function itself is built from periodic sine terms using integer harmonics of z so the terrain tiles seamlessly over the loop while varying freely in x. I'm also planning to scatter squashed boulder instances along the canyon floor, repeating per period.

I should check whether AuraTransformSpec supports rotation, or consider using thin cones instead for the branches.
